Retrieval recall at k, per segmenter

Source: R/doc-segment-quality.R
gr_seg_recall.Rd

For each segmenter, cuts each document of a question-answering reference, ranks its chunks for each question the way the retrieve reader does, and counts the questions whose answer is in one of the first k chunks. This is the share of questions a retrieve reader with top_k = k could answer, before any model reads anything, so segmenters and chunk sizes can be compared for nothing (with the lexical embedder) or for one embedding request per question and segmenter.

Usage

gr_seg_recall(
  reference,
  segmenters,
  k = c(1, 3, 5),
  client = NULL,
  read = list(),
  split = "test"
)

Arguments

reference

A reference from gr_qa_reference().

segmenters

The segmentations: a character vector of segmenter names, or a list of names, gr_segment_spec() objects or named lists of its settings. One spec or one list of settings on its own is one segmentation. Unnamed entries are named by their method and size, as "fixed_32".

k

The cut-offs, whole numbers of at least 1.

client

The client that embeds, or NULL for the lexical embedder (and for segmenters that call no model).

read

Named list of gr_read_spec() settings for the ranking.

split

The split or splits of reference to use.

Value

A data frame with one row per segmenter and k: segmenter, k, hits, questions, recall, no_chunk (questions whose answer is in no chunk), chunks (mean chunks per document) and documents. Attribute ranks holds one row per segmenter and question with the rank of the first chunk holding the answer (NA when none does).

Details

A chunk holds the answer when its text (its source_text, when it has one) contains one of the item's accepted answers, matched as gr_scorer_answer() matches them: case, white space and thousands separators folded, numbers matched whole. An answer cut in two by a chunk edge is in no chunk, and the question counts as a miss at every k; the no_chunk column counts those questions. Unanswerable items and items with no label are left out.

The ranking is cosine similarity on the embeddings client gives (see gr_embed()), blended with BM25 by lexical_blend when the embeddings are lexical, as in gr_read(). read takes those gr_read_spec() settings (lexical_blend, bm25_k1, bm25_b). The mmr and min_score settings of the reader are not applied: this is the ranking alone.

The figures are descriptive. Questions about one document share its chunking, so they are not independent, and no interval is given; compare segmenters on the same questions, and on a split you did not tune on.

See also

gr_seg_pk(), gr_chunk_stats(), hr_benchmark()

Other segmentation functions: gr_check_segmenter(), gr_chunk_stats(), gr_chunks, gr_register_segmenter(), gr_seg_boundaries(), gr_seg_pk(), gr_segment(), gr_segment_spec(), gr_segmenters(), new_chunks()

Examples

old <- gr_options(verbose = FALSE, embedder = "lexical")
doc <- paste("Revenue was 45.2 million dollars in fiscal 2024.",
             "The plant in Leeds made 12,400 units.",
             "Staff numbered 310 at year end.", sep = "\n\n")
ref <- gr_qa_reference(c(rev = "What was revenue?", units = "How many units?"),
                       documents = doc, answers = list("45.2 million", "12,400"),
                       split = "test")
gr_seg_recall(ref, list(sentence = list(method = "sentence", max_tokens = 40),
                        fixed = list(method = "fixed", max_tokens = 32)), k = 1:2)
#>   segmenter k hits questions recall no_chunk chunks documents
#> 1  sentence 1    2         2      1        0      2         1
#> 2  sentence 2    2         2      1        0      2         1
#> 3     fixed 1    2         2      1        0      2         1
#> 4     fixed 2    2         2      1        0      2         1
gr_options(old)
